s: Poh I is associated with heroism (people underrate it)
q: When formerly I heard people detracting from the learning of Confucius or underrating the heroism of Poh I,

s: Yao abdicates in favour of Shun
q: Of old Yao abdicated in favour of Shun, and the latter ruled.

s: Shun rules Middle Kingdom (after Yao's abdication)
q: Of old Yao abdicated in favour of Shun, and the latter ruled.

s: T'ang gets empire (by fighting)
q: T'ang and Wu See ch. xii. got the empire by fighting

s: Spirit of the River travels to ocean (downstream, eastward)
q: Down with the stream he journeyed east, until he reached the ocean.

s: Spirit of the River recognizes Spirit of the Ocean (as inexhaustible and superior)
q: But now that I have looked upon your inexhaustibility--alas for me had I not reached your abode, I should have been for ever a laughing-stock to those of comprehensive enlightenment!

s: well-frog is a creature of a narrower sphere (unable to understand ocean)
q: You cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog,--the creature of a narrower sphere.

s: Spirit of the Ocean receives river (as a speaker seeking instruction)
q: But now that you have emerged from your narrow sphere and have seen the great ocean, you know your own insignificance, and I can speak to you of great principles.

s: ocean is immeasurably superior to mere rivers and brooks (in size and stability)
q: And thus it is immeasurably superior to mere rivers and brooks,--though I would not venture to boast on this account

s: ocean receives streams (without cease)
q: All streams pour into it without cease, yet it does not overflow.

s: walrus envies centipede
q: The walrus envies the centipede;

s: wind envies eye
q: the Wind envies the eye; Which travels even without moving.

s: wind breaks huge trees
q: I can break huge trees and destroy large buildings.

s: wind destroys large buildings
q: I can break huge trees and destroy large buildings.

s: eye envies mind
q: the eye envies the mind;

s: mind comprehends whole universe (past and present alike)
q: Which can comprehend the whole universe, past and present alike.

s: the Sage excel in great things
q: And to excel in great things is given only to the Sages.

s: walrus has legs one
q: I hop about on one leg, but not very successfully.

s: Confucius is surrounded by men of Wei (at K'uang)
q: This is a mistake. "K'uang" was in the Wei State, and it was by the men of Wei that Confucius was surrounded.

s: Confucius plays guitar (without ceasing)
q: Yet he went on playing and singing to his guitar without ceasing.

s: Confucius struggles against failure (for a long time)
q: For a long time I have been struggling against failure, but in vain.

s: Confucius seeks success (for a long time)
q: For a long time I have been seeking success, but in vain.

s: failure is caused by Destiny
q: My destiny is cut out for me.

s: success is opportunity
q: To know that failure is fate and that success is opportunity

s: the Empire has no failures (in the days of Yao and Shun)
q: In the days of Yao and Shun, no man throughout the empire was a failure, though no one was conscious of the gain.

s: centipede has legs many
q: Its many legs and nimble gait.

s: Chieh rules the Empire (in his days)
q: In the days of Chieh and Chou, no man throughout the empire was a success, though no one was conscious of the loss.

s: the Empire has no successes (in the days of Chieh and Chou)
q: In the days of Chieh and Chou, no man throughout the empire was a success, though no one was conscious of the loss.

s: Yu is addressed by Confucius
q: Yu! rest in this. My destiny is cut out for me.

s: Kung Sun Lung is a philosopher (of the Chao State)
q: A philosopher of the Chao State, whose treatise on the "hard and white" etc. is said to be still extant.

s: Kung Sun Lung belongs to State of Chao
q: A philosopher of the Chao State, whose treatise on the "hard and white" etc. is said to be still extant.

s: Kung Sun Lung has treatise on the "hard and white"
q: A philosopher of the Chao State, whose treatise on the "hard and white" etc. is said to be still extant.

s: centipede envies snake
q: the centipede envies the snake;

s: Mou of Wei leans over the table (and sighed)
q: Kung Tzŭ Mou leant over the table and sighed.

s: TAO is studied by Kung Sun Lung (as the TAO of the ancient Sages)
q: When young I studied the TAO of the ancient Sages.

s: Chuang Tzŭ is compared to mosquito (or an ant)
q: to attempt to understand Chuang Tzŭ, is like a mosquito trying to carry a mountain, or an ant to swim a river,--they cannot succeed.

s: Chuang Tzŭ moves in realms below (while soaring to heaven above)
q: Chuang Tzŭ moves in the realms below while soaring to heaven above.

s: Chuang Tzŭ returns to TAO (beginning with chaos)
q: Beginning with chaos, he has gone back to TAO;

s: well-frog lives in old well
q: Have you never heard of the frog in the old well?

s: turtle of the eastern sea is a turtle (of the eastern sea)
q: The frog said to the turtle of the eastern sea,

s: eastern ocean is unaffected by duration of time
q: Not to be affected by duration of time, not to be affected by volume of water,--such is the great happiness of the eastern sea.

s: centipede moves by natural mechanism (without conscious awareness)
q: And so it is that my mechanism works naturally, without my being conscious of the fact.

s: eastern ocean is unaffected by volume of water
q: Not to be affected by duration of time, not to be affected by volume of water,--such is the great happiness of the eastern sea.

s: sacred tortoise is dead three thousand years (approximately)
q: I have heard that in Ch'u there is a sacred tortoise which has been dead now some three thousand years.

s: sacred tortoise is kept in ancestral temple (enclosed in a chest on the altar)
q: And that the prince keeps this tortoise carefully enclosed in a chest on the altar of his ancestral temple.

s: Hui Tzŭ is a prime minister (in the Liang State)
q: Hui Tzŭ was prime minister in the Liang State.

s: Hui Tzŭ belongs to Liang State (as prime minister)
q: Hui Tzŭ was prime minister in the Liang State.

s: phœnix is a bird (of the south)
q: In the south there is a bird. It is a kind of phœnix.

s: phœnix travels between south sea and north sea (when flying)
q: It started from the south sea to fly to the north sea.

s: phœnix alights on wu-t'ung tree (and nowhere else)
q: Except on the _wu-t'ung_ tree, _Eleococca verrucosa_. Williams. it would not alight.

s: bridge over the Hao is over Hao
q: Chuang Tzŭ and Hui Tzŭ had strolled on to the bridge over the Hao,

s: minnows are darting about (in the Hao)
q: See how the minnows are darting about! That is the pleasure of fishes.

s: snake envies wind
q: the snake envies the wind;

s: fishes have pleasure (as inferred from the minnows darting about)
q: See how the minnows are darting about! That is the pleasure of fishes.

s: snake moves without legs
q: Which moves without legs.

s: snake has form
q: I can manage to wriggle along, but I have a form.

s: wind envies eye
q: the Wind envies the eye;

s: perfect happiness is the absence of happiness
q: I make true pleasure to consist in _inaction_, which the world regards as great pain. Thus it has been said, "Perfect happiness is the absence of happiness;

s: Destiny is a pre-arrangement (with fixed limitations)
q: Thus, destiny is a pre-arrangement, just as form has its limitations.

s: the world esteems wealth (among its valued conditions)
q: What the world esteems comprises wealth, rank, old age, and goodness of heart.

s: the world esteems rank (among its valued conditions)
q: What the world esteems comprises wealth, rank, old age, and goodness of heart.

s: the world enjoys comfort (among bodily and sensory pleasures)
q: What it enjoys comprises comfort, rich food, fine clothes, beauty, and music.

s: the world does not esteem poverty (among rejected conditions)
q: What it does not esteem comprises poverty, want of position, early death, and evil behaviour.

s: Heaven does nothing TAO of inaction (yet remains clear)
q: Heaven does nothing; yet it is clear.

s: perfect happiness is sought in TAO of inaction (together with preservation of life)
q: Perfect happiness and preservation of life are to be sought for only in inaction.

s: Earth does nothing TAO of inaction (yet enjoys repose)
q: Earth does nothing; yet it enjoys repose.

s: Chuang Tzŭ is married to Chuang Tzŭ's wife (before her death)
q: When Chuang Tzŭ's wife died, Hui Tzŭ went to condole.

s: Chuang Tzŭ accepts Chuang Tzŭ's wife's death (as a natural transformation)
q: Therefore I refrain.

s: Hui Tzŭ condoles with Chuang Tzŭ (after Chuang Tzŭ's wife's death)
q: When Chuang Tzŭ's wife died, Hui Tzŭ went to condole.

s: hunchback Su is a hunchback (one of two observers of the tombs)
q: A hunchback and a one-legged man were looking at the tombs of departed heroes

s: the skull is a empty skull (bleached but preserving its shape)
q: Chuang Tzŭ one day saw an empty skull, bleached, but still preserving its shape.

s: TAO of inaction produces modifications of things (through Heaven and Earth)
q: From the inaction of these two proceed all the modifications of things.

s: Lieh Tzŭ undertakes Lieh Tzŭ's journey (while eating by the roadside)
q: Lieh Tzŭ, being on a journey, was eating by the roadside, when he saw an old skull.

s: Confucius is sad about Yen Yüan (when Yen Yüan goes east to Ch'i State)
q: When Yen Yüan See p. 179. went eastwards to the Ch'i State, Confucius was sad

s: Yen Yüan goes to Ch'i State (eastwards)
q: When Yen Yüan See p. 179. went eastwards to the Ch'i State, Confucius was sad

s: Confucius fears for Yen Yüan (because he may preach unsuitable doctrines)
q: And I fear lest Hui, on his visit to the prince of Ch'i, should preach the Tao of Yao and Shun

s: TAO of inaction accomplishes nothing left undone (through Heaven and Earth)
q: Heaven and earth do nothing, yet there is nothing which they do not accomplish.

s: happiness is uncertain uncertain (in the human world)
q: As to what the world does and the way in which people are happy now, I know not whether such happiness be real happiness or not.

s: physical well-being is a worldly aim (what the world aims at)
q: What the world aims at is physical well-being

s: life is a loan (that adds dust and dirt to existence)
q: Life is a loan with which the borrower does but add more dust and dirt to the sum total of existence.

s: life is related to death (as day is related to night)
q: Life and death are as day and night;

s: death provides freedom from mortal troubles (according to the skull)
q: In death there are none of these.

s: The Secret of Life is a chapter (Chapter XIX)
q: CHAPTER XIX. THE SECRET OF LIFE.

s: life cannot be declined coming
q: Life comes, and cannot be declined.

s: the prince of Lu asks Ch'ing (about his artistic mystery)
q: And the prince of Lu asked him, saying, "What mystery is there in your art?"

s: horses break down actually broken down
q: in a short time it was announced that the horses had actually broken down

s: life cannot be stopped going
q: It goes, and cannot be stopped.

s: river provides habitat for bird (as a place to swim)
q: let it swim in river or lake

s: the Empire would be at peace peace (if resentment were not carried to objects)
q: And by the extension of this principle, the empire would be at peace; no more confusion of war, no more punishment of death.

s: rebirth is near TAO
q: And he who is re-born is near. To TAO.

s: renunciation of the world suffers no wear and tear body
q: In the first case, the physical body suffers no wear and tear

s: renunciation of the world leaves unharmed vitality
q: in the second, the vitality is left unharmed.

s: body is perfect perfection (when its condition is complete)
q: And he whose physical frame is perfect

s: vitality is in original purity original purity (in the perfect man)
q: and whose vitality is in its original purity

s: Heaven is a parent of all things (with earth)
q: Heaven and earth are the father and mother of all things.

s: The Secret of Life supplements chapter iii
q: [This chapter is supplementary to chapter iii.]

s: Earth is a parent of all things (with Heaven)
q: Heaven and earth are the father and mother of all things.

s: perfection of vitality goes back to God
q: Such perfection of vitality goes back to the minister of God.

s: vitality is a subtle essence (immaterial informing principle united with matter)
q: "Vitality" is the subtle essence, the immaterial informing principle which, united with matter, exhibits the phenomenon of life.

s: Lieh Tzŭ asks Kuan Yin
q: Lieh Tzŭ asked Kuan Yin,

s: Kuan Yin is a sage (according to some accounts)
q: A sage who by some is said to have flourished five or six hundred years before Lieh Tzŭ

s: Kuan Yin is a disciple of Lao Tzŭ (according to some accounts)
q: by others, to have been an immediate disciple of Lao Tzŭ

s: Kuan Yin entrusted with publication of the Tao-Tê-Ching (by Lao Tzŭ, according to some accounts)
q: and to have been entrusted by him with the publication of the _Tao-Tê-Ching_.

s: perfect man walks through solid bodies (without obstruction)
q: The perfect man can walk through solid bodies without obstruction.

s: perfect man passes through fire (without being burnt)
q: He can pass through fire without being burnt.

s: perfect man scales highest heights (without fear)
q: He can scale the highest heights without fear.

s: Kuan Yin attributes perfection to absolute purity (not cunning)
q: "It is because he is in a condition of absolute purity," replied Kuan Yin. "It is not cunning which enables him to dare such feats.

s: perfect man attains formlessness (thereby vanquishing death)
q: But man can attain to formlessness and vanquish death.

s: perfect man nourishes strength (as part of attaining unity)
q: He may bring his nature to a condition of ONE; he may nourish his strength

s: perfect man harmonizes virtue (as part of attaining unity)
q: he may harmonize his virtue

s: perfect man partners with God (after bringing nature to unity and harmonizing virtue)
q: and so put himself into partnership with God.

s: the Sage seeks refuge in God (thereby becoming free from harm)
q: It is in God that the Sage seeks his refuge, and so he is free from harm.

s: soul comes from God
q: The soul is from God

s: Confucius observes hunchback (catching cicadas in a forest)
q: When Confucius was on his way to the Ch'u State, he came to a forest where he saw a hunchback catching cicadas as though with his hand.

s: Confucius teaches singleness of purpose (as inducing concentration of faculties)
q: Confucius looked round at his disciples and said, "Singleness of purpose induces concentration of the faculties.

s: Yen Yüan asks Confucius (about the boatman's skill)
q: Yen Yüan said to Confucius, "When I crossed over the Shang-shên rapid

s: Shang-shên rapid is crossed by Yen Yüan (in a boat)
q: When I crossed over the Shang-shên rapid, the boatman managed his craft with marvellous skill.

s: soul uses as vehicle body (as its vehicle)
q: Man's body its vehicle

s: soul quickens body (thereby producing life)
q: The soul quickening the body is life

s: life is a quickening of the physical body by the soul
q: The soul quickening the body is life

s: Duke Huan travels with Kuan Chung (as charioteer)
q: When Duke Huan was out hunting, with Kuan Chung as his charioteer

s: Kuan Chung is charioteer for Duke Huan (during a hunt)
q: When Duke Huan was out hunting, with Kuan Chung as his charioteer

s: Duke Huan sees bogy (while hunting)
q: he saw a bogy.

s: Huang Tzŭ Kao Ngao is from Ch'i State
q: There came a certain Huang Tzŭ Kao Ngao of the Ch'i State

s: body requires nourishment (for due nourishment)
q: For the due nourishment of our physical frames, certain things are needful.

s: body must not be abandoned care (for preservation of life)
q: For the preservation of life it is necessary that there should be no abandonment of the physical frame.

s: Confucius observes cataract at Lü-liang (with his disciples)
q: Confucius was looking at the cataract at Lü-liang.

s: Chuang Tzŭ travels over a mountain
q: Chuang Tzŭ was travelling over a mountain when he saw a huge tree well covered with foliage.

s: TAO pervades all things (without being seen)
q: TAO pervades all things but is not seen.

s: TAO is a domain (the only domain containing a fixed point amid worldly opposites)
q: Take note, my disciples, that such is to be found only in the domain of TAO.

s: huge tree is a tree (well covered with foliage)
q: Chuang Tzŭ was travelling over a mountain when he saw a huge tree well covered with foliage.

s: huge tree is useless good for nothing (to the woodsman)
q: "This tree," cried Chuang Tzŭ, "by virtue of being good for nothing succeeds in completing its allotted span."

s: goose has attribute cackling or not cackling (the host distinguishes between two geese)
q: "Which shall I kill?" enquired the servant; "the one that cackles or the one that doesn't?"

s: goose is killed death (when it does not cackle)
q: His master told him to kill the one which did not cackle.

s: human element is a hindrance (in oneself)
q: It is the human in ourselves which is our hindrance; and the human in others which causes our sorrow.

s: I Liao advises the prince of Lu (to put away body and skin and purge passion)
q: I would have your Highness put away body and skin alike, and cleansing your heart and purging it of passion, betake yourself to the land where mortality is not.

s: the prince of Lu is skin of your Highness
q: But what crime have they committed? 'Tis their skin which is the cause of their trouble; and is not the State of Lu your Highness' skin?

s: Chuang Tzŭ follows TAO (as a method of living)
q: No praise, no blame; both great and small; changing with the change of time, but ever without special effort; both above and below; making for harmony with surroundings; reaching creation's First Cause; swaying all things and swayed by none;--how then shall such troubles come? This was the method of Shên Nung and Huang Ti.

s: empty boat does not provoke anger (when another boat collides with it)
q: Suppose a boat is crossing a river, and another empty boat is about to collide with it. Even an irritable man would not lose his temper.

s: Pei Kung Shê is a minister (to Duke Ling of Wei)
q: Pei Kung Shê, minister to Duke Ling of Wei, levied contributions for making bells.

s: Pei Kung Shê levies contributions for bells (without resentment or gratitude)
q: I showed no resentment towards the unwilling, nor gratitude towards those who gave. Every one subscribed what he liked; and thus in my daily collection of subscriptions, no injury was done.

s: Confucius experiences siege between Ch'ên and Ts'ai (while hemmed in and without food)
q: When Confucius was hemmed in between Ch'ên and Ts'ai, he passed seven days without food.

s: Chuang Tzŭ has relationship with old friend (as a guest)
q: When Chuang Tzŭ left the mountain, he put up at the house of an old friend.

s: Confucius fears death
q: "Do you fear death, Sir?" enquired Jen. "I do," said Confucius.

s: Confucius sings Confucius's song of Piao Shih (during the siege between Ch'ên and Ts'ai)
q: When Confucius was hemmed in between Ch'ên and Ts'ai and had gone seven days without food, then, holding in his left hand a piece of dry wood and in his right hand a dry stick, he sang a ballad of Piao Shih.

s: Confucius asks Tzŭ Sang Hu
q: Confucius asked Tzŭ Sang Hu, See ch. vi. saying, "I have been twice expelled from Lu. My tree was cut down in Sung. I have been tabooed in Wei. I am a failure in Shang and Chou. I was surrounded between Ch'ên and Ts'ai

s: Tzŭ Sang Hu teaches Confucius (that divine bonds exceed material ones)
q: And so it is that in trouble and calamity mere money questions are neglected, while we ever cling nearer to that which is from God.

s: Yen Yüan is a disciple (of Confucius)
q: Yen Hui, who was standing by in a respectful attitude, thereupon began to turn his eyes about him;

s: Yen Yüan questions Confucius (about God, man, and adaptation)
q: "Pray, Sir, what do you mean," asked Yen Hui, "by saying that it is easy to escape injury from God?"

s: God is a source (of man)
q: That man is," replied Confucius, "is from God. That God is, is also from God.

s: God is one with man (in the relation of man and God)
q: Man and God are ONE.

s: Chuang Tzŭ is hindered by human element (in worldly life)
q: It is the human in ourselves which is our hindrance; and the human in others which causes our sorrow.

s: Tiao-ling is a park (where Chuang Tzŭ wandered)
q: When Chuang Tzŭ was wandering in the park at Tiao-ling, he saw a strange bird which came from the south.

s: strange bird has wingspan seven feet
q: Its wings were seven feet across.

s: strange bird has eyes an inch in circumference (each eye)
q: Its eyes were an inch in circumference.

s: strange bird forgets its own nature (because focused on prey)
q: And this it was which had caused the bird to forget its own nature.

s: Yang Chu is a philosopher (also called Yang Chu)
q: When Yang Tzŭ Yang Chu. See ch. viii. went to the Sung State, he passed a night at

s: Yang Chu teaches be virtuous (without being consciously so)
q: "Note this, my disciples!" cried Yang Tzŭ. "Be virtuous, but without being consciously so; and wherever you go, you will be beloved."

s: adaptation leads to rank and power (when adapting to surroundings)
q: If one begins," replied Confucius, "by adaptation to surroundings, rank and power follow without cease.

s: Destiny is a cause of events (as implied by the episode's caption)
q: A legend at the side reads,--"All is Destiny!"

s: the dilemma of usefulness rests between the two
q: "I rest," replied Chuang Tzŭ with a smile, "halfway between the two.

s: death is a burial (in the natural order of Established-Virtue)
q: Life is for enjoyment; death, for burial.

s: Chuang Tzŭ experiences expulsion from Lu (twice)
q: I have been twice expelled from Lu.

s: Chuang Tzŭ experiences siege between Ch'ên and Ts'ai
q: I was surrounded between Ch'ên and Ts'ai.

s: Chuang Tzŭ is poor poverty (without misery because he has TAO)
q: poverty, not misery," replied Chuang Tzŭ. "A man who has TAO cannot be miserable

s: Chuang Tzŭ wears cotton clothes with patches (as a sign of poverty)
q: Chuang Tzŭ put on cotton clothes with patches in them, and arranging his girdle and tieing on his shoes, To keep them from falling off. went to see the

s: TAO is a way (the great way)
q: How much more then those who have the great WAY?

s: T'ien Tzŭ Fang attends upon Prince Wên of Wei (as attendant)
q: T'ien Tzŭ Fang was in attendance upon Prince Wên of Wei.

s: Perfect Man is a man (in appearance)
q: In appearance, a man; in reality, God.

s: Perfect Man is unconditioned unconditioned (himself)
q: Unconditioned himself, he falls in with the conditioned, to his own greater glory.

s: Perfect Man tolerates others (while remaining pure)
q: Pure himself, he can still tolerate others.

s: Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ is a sage (from the south)
q: When Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ "A sage from the south," as the commentators say, anticipating the "Middle Kingdom" below.

s: Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ visits Lu (on journeys to and from Ch'i)
q: When Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ "A sage from the south," as the commentators say, anticipating the "Middle Kingdom" below. was on his way to Ch'i, he broke his journey in Lu.

s: Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ judges lacking Middle Kingdom (knowledge of the human heart)
q: I have heard that the gentlemen of the Middle Kingdom are experts in ceremonies and obligations, but wanting in knowledge of the human heart.

s: Lu contains scholars (many who wear scholars' robes, according to Duke Ai)
q: "We have many scholars, Sir, in Lu, but few of your school."

s: Confucius recognizes TAO (in men of this kind without speech)
q: With such men as these," replied Confucius, you have only to look, and TAO abides. There is no room for speech."

s: Confucius is addressed by Yen Yüan (as master)
q: Yen Yüan See p. 179. asked Confucius, saying, "Master, when you go at a walk, I go at a walk.

s: T'ien Tzŭ Fang praises Ch'i Kung (repeatedly)
q: He kept on praising Ch'i Kung, until at length Prince Wên said, "Is Ch'i Kung your tutor?"

s: Yen Yüan follows Confucius (in speech, argument, and preaching TAO)
q: as you speak, I speak. As you argue, I argue. As you preach TAO, so I preach TAO.

s: Yen Yüan cannot understand Confucius (how he influences people without striving)
q: I cannot understand how this is so."

s: Life depends on that (for death or for life)
q: And every human being has that upon which he depends for death or for life.

s: mind perishes with body (without due modification)
q: So that the mind perishes with the body.

s: Lao Tzŭ is visited by Confucius (while wandering in the unborn)
q: Confucius went to see Lao Tzŭ.

s: Lao Tzŭ wanders in the unborn (in a trammelled state of mind)
q: "I was wandering," replied Lao Tzŭ, "in the unborn."

s: the unborn precedes Life (as the state before birth)
q: Reflecting upon the state of man before his birth into the world.

s: T'ien Tzŭ Fang has tutor Tung Kuo Shun Tzŭ
q: "I have," replied Tzŭ Fang.

s: Heaven emanates passivity (above)
q: Passivity emanates from heaven above; activity proceeds from earth beneath.

s: Earth produces activity (beneath Heaven)
q: Passivity emanates from heaven above; activity proceeds from earth beneath.

s: First Cause produces THE UNIVERSE (possibly)
q: There may be a First Cause, but we never see his form.

s: First Cause fills space (through its report)
q: His report fills space.

s: THE UNIVERSE results from interaction of the perfect Negative principle and perfect Positive principle (through harmony)
q: The interaction of the two results in that harmony by which all things are produced.

s: Duke Ai of Lu believes lu has scholars (many)
q: "We have many scholars, Sir, in Lu, but few of your school."

s: T'ien Tzŭ Fang regards as perfect Tung Kuo Shun Tzŭ (his tutor)
q: "He is perfect," replied Tzŭ Fang.

s: scholars wear scholars' robes (not necessarily those with TAO)
q: But scholars who have TAO do not necessarily wear robes; neither does the wearing of robes necessarily mean that a scholar has TAO.

s: scholars' robes do not indicate TAO (necessarily)
q: neither does the wearing of robes necessarily mean that a scholar has TAO.

s: Po Li Ch'i disdains rank and power
q: Rank and power had no charms for Po Li Ch'i.

s: Wên Wang employs old man of Tsang (in the administration of government)
q: So Wên Wang wished to employ him in the administration of government, but feared lest his own ministers, uncles, and brothers, might object.

s: old man of Tsang administers administration of government (for Wên Wang)
q: So the old man of Tsang was received and entrusted with the administration.

s: old man of Tsang changes existing statutes (none)
q: He altered none of the existing statutes. He issued no unjust regulations.

s: old man of Tsang becomes Grand Tutor (appointed by Wên Wang)
q: So Wên Wang appointed the old man Grand Tutor;

s: Wên Wang has dream of Wên Wang (about the Sage and old gentleman of Tsang)
q: I once dreamt that a Sage of a black colour and with a large beard, riding upon a parti-coloured horse with red stockings on one side, appeared and instructed me to place the administration in the hands of the old gentleman of Tsang, promising that the people would benefit greatly thereby."

s: Lieh Tzŭ instructs Po Hun Wu Jên (in archery)
q: Lieh Yü K'ou _Or_ Lieh Tzŭ. See ch. i. instructed Po Hun Wu Jên See ch. v. in archery.

s: TAO is not reached by superficial worker
q: TAO is not to be reached by the superficial worker, or by such as value the distinctions of this world.

s: Note on the Philosophy of Chaps. i-vii is a philosophical note
q: _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii

s: Western philosophy provides preconceptions (for interpreting the system)
q: It is difficult to see how one who writes not only in ignorance of Chinese modes of thought, but with the preconceptions of Western philosophy, can really help much towards the understanding of an admittedly obscure system

s: East and West have parallelisms of thought and reasoning
q: But an attempt to point out parallelisms of thought and reasoning between East and West may be of use in two ways.

s: Greek philosophy contains parallelisms with Eastern systems (without requiring theories of derivation)
q: And the result has been that we have learned to put aside theories of derivation, and to content ourselves with tracing the evolution of reason and of rational problems, and to expect parallelisms even where the circumstances are widely different.

s: Aristotle teaches the mean (as an ethical doctrine)
q: it was said with reason that the Aristotelian doctrine of "the mean" was the ripe fruit of the practical inquiries of the Greeks, and was the ethical counterpart of their artistic development.

s: Chuang Tzŭ is a idealist (and mystic)
q: But Chuang Tzŭ has nothing of the sceptic in him. He is an idealist and a mystic

s: Chuang Tzŭ teaches relativity (of size, space, and time)
q: For size is relative.

s: sense knowledge is commonplace in Greek (and modern philosophy)
q: This doctrine of "relativity," which is a commonplace in Greek as it is in modern philosophy

s: Chuang Tzŭ rejects sense knowledge (as an adequate basis of knowledge)
q: His exposure of false and superficial thinking looks at first like the destruction of knowledge.

s: Chuang Tzŭ teaches Identity of Contraries (in chapter II)
q: It is impossible in reading this chapter on "The Identity of Contraries" not to be reminded of Heracleitus.

s: Identity of Contraries unites contraries (within the One)
q: the sage sees the many disappearing in the One, in which subjective and objective, positive and negative, here and there, somewhere and nowhere, meet and blend.

s: Chuang Tzŭ resembles Heracleitus (in the conception of a living unity)
q: But it seems to me that the "One" of Chuang Tzŭ is not the dead Unit of Eleaticism, which resulted from the thinking away of differences, but the living Unity of Heracleitus, in which contraries co-exist.

s: Heracleitus teaches the unity of all things (through reason)
q: "Listen," says Heracleitus, "not to me, but to reason, and confess the true wisdom that 'All things are ONE.'"

s: Heracleitus teaches the unity of opposites (as the structure of the world)
q: The world is a unity of opposing forces

s: Heracleitus regards sense knowledge (as unreliable)
q: For they trust to their senses, which are "false witnesses."

s: Chuang Tzŭ teaches TAO (as the path from seeming to truth)
q: he teaches them how to pass from the seeming to the true.

s: Confucius teaches fasting of the heart (as distinct from bodily fasting)
q: "Cultivate _fasting_;--not bodily fasting, but the fasting of the heart."

s: Chuang Tzŭ teaches the usefulness of being useless

s: Confucianism is limited to the finite (in practice)

s: Taoism seeks the Absolute (the Infinite and the Eternal)
q: And the sage seeks for the Absolute, the Infinite, the Eternal. He seeks to attain to TAO.

s: Chuang Tzŭ is a mystic (especially in chapters VI and VII)
q: It is here that we reach (in chaps. vi, vii) what properly constitutes the _mysticism_ of Chuang Tzŭ.

s: Chuang Tzŭ teaches abstraction from self (as the road to Tao)
q: Abstraction from self, then, is the road which leads to TAO (chap. vi).

s: TAO is greater than God (in Chuang Tzŭ's teaching)
q: For they had attained to TAO, and TAO is greater than God.

s: TAO orders the universe (through eternal principles)
q: The sun and moon, and the Great Bear are kept in their courses by TAO.

s: Taoism contains antinomianism (as do mystical systems generally)
q: In Chuang Tzŭ, as in all mystics, there is an element of antinomianism.

s: Christianity teaches inwardness (and resistance to limitation to visible things)
q: For Christianity also teaches _inwardness_, and, in common with all idealism, resents the delimitation of human life and knowledge to "the things which are seen."

s: Christianity and Taoism comparison contrasts Confucianism (through Taoism's opposition to a merely practical system)
q: In its opposition to a mere practical system like Confucianism, Taoism must have appealed to those deeper instincts of humanity to which Buddhism appealed some centuries later.
